summary: For Muslims, who are most residents, Islamic law fixes the heirs' shares and a will can dispose of at most one third. Non-Muslims are believed to have freedom of testation. Brunei has trust law, including an international trusts order, but I found no foundation statute and the Hague Trusts Convention is not in force.
reserved_share: Muslims: Islamic fixed shares (faraid); a will may pass at most one third of the net estate to non-heirs unless the heirs consent. This is the general Sharia rule; the Brunei statute and article were not retrieved.
family_claims: Non-Muslims: I did not confirm whether Brunei has a family-provision statute.
foreign_law_note: Muslim estates follow Islamic law and Syariah courts, so no choice of another law. For non-Muslim foreigners I could not source the conflict rule; Brunei applies English common law principles, which would send movables to the law of domicile and land to Brunei law, but this is not confirmed.
trust_note: Brunei is not on the HCCH status table for the Trusts Convention. Trusts exist under common law and the Trustees Act, and the International Trusts Order 2000 offers an offshore trust regime (not retrieved this session). I found no private foundation statute; the 'no' is the absence of one, not a verified prohibition. No inheritance tax was checked.
open_questions: Confirm Brunei's Wills Act and Intestate Succession Act chapter numbers and whether a family-provision claim exists for non-Muslims.
Confirm the International Trusts Order 2000 is in force and current.
Confirm no private foundation law exists (Brunei has no known foundation statute).
Source the Islamic Family Law / Syariah provisions for the one-third limit in Brunei itself.
Trusts/foundations marked unclear: the research found no source either way, which is not evidence that no such law exists.
